title: The poor
hookLine: know one poor person by name
tomorrow: what do grandparents carry that nobody else can?

cards: Notice who gets a name in a news story: the CEO, the senator, the team owner. The people sleeping under the overpass get a plural. Jesus tells a story in Luke that flips it.

A rich man dresses in purple and fine linen and feasts every day. And in the Douay-Rheims Bible, there is "a certain beggar, named Lazarus," lying at his gate, covered in sores, longing for the crumbs from the table.
The rich man has no name. The poor man does. Why?

teach.h: THE RICH MAN HAS NO NAME.
teach.b: Luke never names the rich man. The old Latin Bible just calls him dives, which means a rich man, and over time people turned that word into a name. He's a type.
Lazarus is a person. Here's the detail to tell a friend tonight.
Both men die, and the rich man, in torment, looks up and asks Abraham to send Lazarus with a drop of water. Send Lazarus.
He knew his name the whole time. Every day he walked past a man whose name he knew, and never crossed his own gate. The story never says he kicked him or cursed him.

It says he feasted, and Lazarus lay there. Luke even adds that the dogs came and licked his sores. The street dogs came closer to Lazarus than the man inside the house ever did, and the man inside had his name ready.
The Catechism reads this parable when it teaches about love for the poor, and Catholic teaching speaks of a love of preference for them.
Saint John puts the test plainly: love not in word or in tongue, but in deed and in truth.
A name is where the deed starts. It turns the poor, a plural, back into one person with a face, a story, and a voice you'd recognize.

how: Catholics hear the parable of the rich man and Lazarus at Mass, and count feeding the hungry among the corporal works of mercy.

people who earn less than the town's average
people in need, each with a name and a face

games.q: a man asks for change at the same corner on your way to work, every day. what does Luke 16 nudge you toward?
o: give coins each time, but keep walking so it isn't awkward.
donate online to a shelter instead; it helps more people.
learn his name, and use it the next time you pass.
games.why: in Luke the poor man is the one with a name, and the rich man knew it but never crossed his gate. a name is where the deed starts.

practice: If you have a piece of bread or anything to eat nearby, take one small bite and taste it slowly, the way Lazarus longed for crumbs.

While you taste it, bring to mind someone you pass who goes without: the man at the corner, the woman at the bus stop. If you know their name, say it softly. If you don't, let that be the thing you'd like to learn.

wordCard.voice: The poor. Not a plural in a headline, but people with names, like Lazarus at the gate. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, Luke 16:19 in the Vulgate: a rich man. a description that people later used as a name.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: by name, the way Jesus told the story at the gate. Off you go.
